clue.text: Game is my sole possession

blocks.note: first meaning: the property-trading board game
second meaning: exclusive ownership or control of something

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that a particular game belongs to them alone.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a possessive child guarding a toy; the two halves are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The board game shares its name with the economic term for exclusive control of a market or thing.

clue.text: Veto suggested for one avoiding whipping

blocks.note: setter's reading: read the answer as an instruction, its first word telling you to loosen the letters of its second, and the result spells 'Veto'
surface reading: a parliamentary ballot in which members are not told by party officials which side to back

explanation.surface: A politician hints at a veto in a ballot where party discipline is relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: FREE VOTE would be wordplay for 'veto', with FREE loosening the letters of VOTE. In Parliament, whips are officials who make members back the party line; on a conscience matter the whip is lifted.
explanation.definitionFit: A Commons ballot where members follow conscience rather than party instruction escapes the usual whipping by officials.

clue.text: Smallest digit? I beg to differ

definitions.text: Smallest digit? I beg to differ

indicators.note: to differ is to be other than as given, so the letters come out in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a digit is the smallest and another person politely disagrees.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: asked whether a toe is the smallest digit, the answer protests that this one is the largest.
explanation.definitionFit: Toes are digits, and the largest toe on the foot is the one that would object to being called smallest.

clue.text: Quickly produce stunning victory in cup match

blocks.note: first meaning: to make something fast and without much care, as a phrasal verb
second meaning: a win by flooring the opponent, and also the elimination format of a cup competition

explanation.surface: A team rattles off a dazzling win in a cup tie.
explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is a verb phrase written as two words, knock out; the second is the noun written as one.
explanation.definitionFit: To dash off work is a phrasal verb with this form, while the noun names a stunning blow or eliminating contest.

clue.text: Deceptive reliance on the second Queen Mary, say

indicators.note: something deceptive is not what it seems, so the letters disguise their true arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone warns that trusting the runner-up Queen Mary is misguided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The second' seems to attach to 'reliance on', but it belongs with 'Queen Mary': the Queen Mary 2 is a Cunard ship. 'Say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Queen Mary 2 is a famous Cunard passenger ship, an example of a large vessel crossing seas on scheduled routes.

clue.text: Society regularises rugby code

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for society
to even something out is to make it regular

explanation.surface: A sporting body standardises the rules of rugby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularises' reads as part of the surface sentence but supplies a verb meaning makes level.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven-a-side rugby is a distinct form of the game, played in short matches and at the Olympics.

clue.text: Staying at school and getting on

blocks.note: first meaning: living at a residential school during term
second meaning: climbing aboard a train, ship or plane

explanation.surface: A pupil remains at school and grows older.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' looks like ageing or progressing, but it means stepping aboard a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils who live in at a residential school are described this way, and passengers entering a plane do the same.

clue.text: Accepted as authority and passed

blocks.note: first meaning: followed something as a guide, as in following the rule book
second meaning: elapsed, as time does

explanation.walkthrough: To go by a rule is to treat it as the authority; days that have elapsed have also done this.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both followed a guide or rule and elapsed or moved past, as years do.

clue.text: Sound from horse in pound

blocks.note: first meaning: a soft, low whinny
second meaning: British slang for one pound sterling

explanation.surface: A horse makes a noise while shut in an animal enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like an animal enclosure; it is the money. In British slang a nicker is one pound.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle whinny from a horse has this name, and in British slang it is also one pound sterling.

clue.text: See 2 Down
I’m drunk, ruining winter coat

definitions.note: the answer speaks in the first person: it is a drink

indicators.note: ruining something wrecks its shape, so the letters are wrecked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tipsy reveller confesses to having spoiled a winter coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm drunk' reads as intoxicated, but it is a mixer saying it gets drunk, that is, swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: This quinine-flavoured fizzy mixer is a beverage, so it could truthfully say people swallow it.

clue.text: Item left in car

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
a coupe is a two-door car

explanation.surface: Something has been forgotten in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Item' looks like a lost object, but it means two people in a relationship, as in 'they're an item'.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people romantically involved are informally called an item, which is the same as a pair in a relationship.

clue.text: One extravagantly praising various grain types

indicators.note: various means of several kinds, so the letters can be arranged in another way

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone gushes over a range of cereals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Various grain types' reads as a list of cereals being praised, but it is just the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A panegyric is a formal speech of lavish tribute, and the person who delivers such eulogies is named from it.

clue.text: Vain, going round in socks?

blocks.note: first meaning: futile, an old word for useless
second meaning, playful: someone walking about in socks has no footwear on

explanation.surface: A conceited person wanders around in socks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vain' looks like conceited but means futile; the question mark flags the jokey literal reading of the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: The literary adjective means unavailing or to no purpose, and literally describes someone lacking footwear.

clue.text: Lethal agent ruins nice day

indicators.note: to ruin something is to wreck its form, so the letters fall into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A deadly spy spoils an otherwise pleasant day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agent' suggests an assassin, but it is a chemical agent, a poison.
explanation.definitionFit: This fast-acting poison is a deadly chemical substance, the classic toxin of murder mysteries.

clue.text: Clean room no benefit for one out all winter

blocks.note: to do a room is to clean it
RM is the abbreviation for room
nothing, zero, the letter O
use as a noun means benefit, as in 'what's the use?'

explanation.surface: Tidying a room earns nothing for someone who is away all winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clean room' reads as one phrase, but it is two pieces. 'Out' means unconscious: this rodent sleeps through the cold months.
explanation.definitionFit: This small rodent hibernates for much of the year, so it is famously asleep, dead to the world, through the cold season.

clue.text: Offer support, but fail to intervene

blocks.note: first meaning: remain loyal to someone
second meaning: watch without doing anything

explanation.surface: Someone promises help but then does nothing when it matters.
explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings are almost opposites, which the surface turns into a story of a disappointing friend.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both remain loyal to a person and look on passively while something happens.

clue.text: Receptacle for cash in low-class prison

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: base means of low rank or quality
a till is a shop's cash drawer

explanation.surface: Money is kept in a box inside a grim jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low-class prison' reads as one phrase; the adjective is the outer piece and only 'prison' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was the Paris fortress-jail stormed in 1789, and the name is used generally for a gaol.

clue.text: Vulcan a fool? Be serious!

blocks.note: Vulcan is the setter, who refers to himself
taken as written
a nit is a silly person

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea that the setter could be foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: Vulcan is this puzzle's setter, so his name stands for 'me'. NIT is short for nitwit.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to be sincere about what they say is the same as demanding that they are not joking.

clue.text: Hang on – that is what my wife wears

blocks.note: to linger is to stay on
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone pauses to point out their wife's clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang on' sounds like a request to wait, but it supplies a verb meaning stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Women's underwear and nightclothes go by this French-derived name, garments a wife might put on.

clue.text: Receptive when it’s scorching

blocks.note: first meaning: of a female animal, ready to mate
second meaning, literally: during hot weather

explanation.walkthrough: 'Receptive' looks like open to ideas, but here it is the animal sense of being ready to mate.
explanation.definitionFit: A female mammal in her fertile period is described this way, and the phrase also literally means during a hot spell.

clue.text: This is why I say your views are unacceptable

indicators.note: saying something means voicing it, so the piece goes by its spoken form

blocks.note: 'here's' is a contraction pointing out something present
the letter Y is pronounced like the question word

explanation.surface: Someone explains why they reject another person's opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This is why' reads as the start of an explanation; it is the wordplay, with Y standing in for the word that sounds like it.
explanation.definitionFit: Belief contrary to accepted doctrine is condemned by authorities as unorthodox, so the holder's opinions are rejected.

clue.text: Boisterous youngster’s Orkney retreat?

blocks.note: Hoy is one of the Orkney islands off northern Scotland
a den is a private hideaway

explanation.surface: A rowdy child has a hideaway in the Scottish isles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orkney' stands for one of its islands; the question mark warns that the clue picks one example.
explanation.definitionFit: This old-fashioned word names a high-spirited, rowdy girl, a lively young tomboy.

clue.text: Vegetable cooking, no wine

blocks.note: chard is a leafy vegetable
food that is cooking is on
nay is an old word for no

explanation.surface: Someone cooks vegetables without adding wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking' wants to be an anagram signal, but there is nothing to rearrange: it means ON, as in the dinner is on.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a white grape variety and the dry white drink made from it, a popular vintage.

clue.text: Lifting this aboard requires muscle from the start and amazing stamina

definitions.text: Lifting this aboard requires muscle from the start and amazing stamina

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
amazing means astonishing or bewildering, so the letters are thrown into confusion

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hoisting a heavy spar onto a ship takes strength and endurance.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: getting a ship's principal mast on board needs muscle and stamina, and the wordplay uses both words.
explanation.definitionFit: The tallest, principal spar of a sailing vessel is huge and heavy, so lifting it aboard takes great strength.

clue.text: See 24 Across
US state 75% the size of another

indicators.note: three quarters of the size means a quarter is lost, so some letters are dropped

blocks.note: another US state, eight letters long, whose last six letters form a second state

explanation.surface: One American state is three quarters as big as a neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Size' suggests area, but it is the length of the name: dropping AR, two of ARKANSAS's eight letters, leaves six, which is 75%.
explanation.definitionFit: This Midwestern plains territory is one of the fifty constituent members of the American union.

clue.text: These people welcome girl back in region of Greece

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in the opposite direction
to welcome is to take someone in, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a pronoun for a group of people
a lass is a girl, especially in Scotland and northern England

explanation.surface: A group of locals greets a returning girl in part of Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal but is only a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a historic area of central-eastern Greece, a plain around Larissa and Volos.
